content: Passive voice is used when the receiver of an action is more important than the person or thing doing the action. The basic form is be + past participle.
examples: The room is cleaned every day.
English is spoken in many countries.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the verb be before the past participle.
Using the base verb instead of the past participle.

content: Present simple passive describes regular actions, facts, and routines where the object receives the action. Use am, is, or are with the past participle.
examples: The office is cleaned every evening.
These books are used in class.
common_mistakes: Using do or does in affirmative passive sentences.
Writing is clean instead of is cleaned.

content: Past simple passive describes completed actions in the past where the receiver of the action is the focus. Use was or were with the past participle.
examples: The window was broken yesterday.
The letters were sent this morning.
common_mistakes: Using was or were with the base verb.
Choosing was for plural subjects.

content: Future passive describes actions that will happen to the subject in the future. Use will be with the past participle.
examples: The results will be announced tomorrow.
The package will be delivered next week.
common_mistakes: Omitting be after will.
Using will be with the base verb instead of the past participle.

content: Use by to mention the agent in a passive sentence when the doer is important or surprising. If the doer is obvious or unimportant, the by phrase is often omitted.
formula: subject + be + past participle + by + agent
examples: The song was written by a famous composer.
The building was designed by a young architect.
common_mistakes: Using from instead of by for the agent.
Adding a by phrase when the agent is not useful.

content: A relative clause gives more information about a noun. It usually begins with a relative pronoun such as who, which, that, where, or whose.
examples: The man who lives next door is a doctor.
This is the book that I bought yesterday.
common_mistakes: Using who for things.
Using which for people in basic identifying clauses.

content: Use who in a relative clause when the noun refers to a person and the person is the subject of the relative clause.
examples: The teacher who helped me was very kind.
A student who studies regularly usually improves.
common_mistakes: Using which for a person.
Leaving out who when it is the subject of the relative clause.

content: Use which in a relative clause when the noun refers to a thing, an animal, or an idea.
examples: The laptop which I bought is very light.
The movie which won the prize was excellent.
common_mistakes: Using who for objects.
Confusing which with where for places.

content: Use where in a relative clause when the noun refers to a place and the clause describes what happens in that place.
examples: This is the cafe where we first met.
I visited the village where my grandparents lived.
common_mistakes: Using where for time expressions.
Using where when which plus a preposition is needed.

content: A defining relative clause identifies exactly which person or thing we mean. It is essential to the meaning and does not use commas.
examples: The woman who called you is my manager.
The file that you need is on the desk.
common_mistakes: Adding commas around a defining relative clause.
Removing the relative clause when it is needed to identify the noun.

content: Zero conditional describes facts, general truths, and regular results. Use present simple in both clauses.
examples: If water reaches 100 degrees Celsius, it boils.
If people exercise regularly, they feel healthier.
common_mistakes: Using will in the result clause for general facts.
Using past tense for a general truth.

content: First conditional describes a real possible situation in the future and its likely result. Use present simple after if and will in the result clause.
formula: if + present simple, will + base verb
examples: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay home.
If you study tonight, you will pass the quiz.
common_mistakes: Using will directly after if.
Using past tense in the if clause for a real future possibility.

content: Second conditional describes unreal or unlikely situations in the present or future. Use past simple in the if clause and would with the base verb in the result clause.
formula: if + past simple, would + base verb
examples: If I had more time, I would learn French.
If she lived closer, she would visit more often.
common_mistakes: Using would in the if clause.
Using present simple for an unreal situation.

content: Third conditional describes unreal past situations and imagined past results. Use past perfect in the if clause and would have with the past participle in the result clause.
formula: if + past perfect, would have + past participle
examples: If I had known about the meeting, I would have attended.
If they had left earlier, they would have caught the train.
common_mistakes: Using would have in the if clause.
Using past simple instead of past perfect.

content: Reported speech tells someone what another person said without quoting the exact words. Tenses, pronouns, and time expressions often change.
examples: She said that she was tired.
He told me that he liked the book.
common_mistakes: Keeping all pronouns the same as direct speech.
Forgetting to change the tense after a past reporting verb.

content: When reporting statements with a past reporting verb, present simple often changes to past simple, and present continuous often changes to past continuous.
examples: Direct: I work here. Reported: She said that she worked there.
Direct: I am studying. Reported: He said that he was studying.
common_mistakes: Using told without an object.
Not changing here to there when the context changes.

content: Reported questions use statement word order after the question word or after if/whether. Do not use the auxiliary question order.
examples: She asked where I lived.
He asked if I could help him.
common_mistakes: Keeping question word order in reported questions.
Forgetting if or whether for yes/no questions.

content: Present simple describes habits, routines, facts, and general truths. Add s or es to the verb with he, she, and it in affirmative sentences.
examples: She studies English every day.
The sun rises in the east.
common_mistakes: Forgetting s or es with third person singular subjects.
Using present continuous for permanent facts.

content: Present continuous describes actions happening now or around now. Use am, is, or are with the -ing form of the verb.
examples: I am reading a book now.
They are preparing for the test this week.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the verb be.
Using present continuous with stative verbs too often.

content: Past simple describes completed actions in the past. Regular verbs usually end in -ed, while irregular verbs have special past forms.
examples: We visited the museum yesterday.
She bought a new notebook last week.
common_mistakes: Using the base verb after a past time expression.
Adding -ed to irregular verbs.

content: Present perfect connects the past with the present. Use have or has with the past participle for experiences, recent actions, or unfinished time periods.
examples: I have visited Singapore twice.
She has finished her homework.
common_mistakes: Using present perfect with a finished past time such as yesterday.
Using have with he, she, or it.

content: Use at for clock times, on for days and dates, and in for months, years, seasons, and longer periods.
formula: at + time, on + day/date, in + month/year/season
examples: The meeting starts at 9 a.m.
We have class on Monday.
She was born in 2005.
common_mistakes: Using in with specific days.
Using on with clock times.

content: Use in for enclosed or larger areas, on for surfaces, and at for specific points or locations.
formula: in + area/container, on + surface, at + point
examples: The keys are in the bag.
The picture is on the wall.
I am waiting at the bus stop.
common_mistakes: Using on for enclosed spaces.
Using in for a specific meeting point.

content: Some adjectives, verbs, and nouns are commonly followed by fixed prepositions. These combinations should be learned as chunks.
examples: She is interested in science.
He depends on his team.
They are responsible for the project.
common_mistakes: Translating prepositions directly from Vietnamese.
Using about after interested instead of in.

content: Airport vocabulary includes boarding pass, gate, luggage, passport, security check, and departure. These words are useful for basic travel conversations.
examples: Please show your boarding pass at the gate.
My luggage is too heavy.
common_mistakes: Confusing luggage with language.
Using ticket when boarding pass is more specific.

content: Hotel vocabulary includes reservation, reception, check in, check out, room key, single room, double room, and accommodation.
examples: I have a reservation for two nights.
What time is check-out?
common_mistakes: Confusing reservation with preservation.
Using house when hotel room is intended.

content: Negative present simple passive puts not after am, is, or are. It describes actions that do not happen to the subject.
examples: The door is not locked during the day.
These files are not shared with everyone.
common_mistakes: Putting not before the subject.
Using do not before a passive verb.

content: Present simple passive questions place am, is, or are before the subject.
examples: Are these emails sent automatically?
Is the classroom cleaned every day?
common_mistakes: Using do or does in passive questions.
Forgetting to move the be verb before the subject.

content: Negative past simple passive uses was not or were not with the past participle.
examples: The tickets were not printed.
The window was not repaired yesterday.
common_mistakes: Using did not before the passive verb.
Using the base verb after was or were.

content: Modal passive uses a modal verb followed by be and the past participle. It is useful for rules, obligations, and possibilities.
examples: The form must be submitted today.
The room can be booked online.
common_mistakes: Omitting be after the modal.
Using modal plus past participle without be.

content: Present perfect passive focuses on completed actions with present relevance. Use have or has been with the past participle.
examples: The documents have been checked.
The password has been changed.
common_mistakes: Using have been with a base verb.
Forgetting been in perfect passive sentences.

content: To change active to passive, move the object to subject position, choose the correct form of be, and use the past participle.
formula: object + be + past participle + by + agent
examples: They clean the office. -> The office is cleaned.
A chef cooked the meal. -> The meal was cooked by a chef.
common_mistakes: Keeping the active subject as the main subject.
Not matching the tense of be to the active verb.

content: Some verbs with two objects can form two passive sentences. The person object is often used as the passive subject.
examples: She was given a prize.
A prize was given to her.
common_mistakes: Dropping one object completely.
Using to after the person-object passive subject.

content: Reporting verbs can be used in passive structures to present general beliefs or reports in formal writing.
examples: It is believed that the painting is valuable.
The project is expected to finish soon.
common_mistakes: Using active informal phrasing in formal reports.
Mixing it is said and subject is said forms incorrectly.

content: The get passive is common in informal English, especially for events that happen unexpectedly or negatively.
examples: My phone got stolen.
He got promoted last month.
common_mistakes: Using get passive in very formal contexts too often.
Using get with a base verb instead of a past participle.

content: The agent is often omitted in passive sentences when it is unknown, obvious, or not important.
examples: My bike was stolen.
English is spoken here.
common_mistakes: Adding by someone when the agent is not useful.
Thinking every passive sentence needs a by phrase.

content: That can refer to people or things in defining relative clauses. It is common in everyday English.
examples: The book that you recommended was useful.
The person that called you is outside.
common_mistakes: Using that in all non-defining clauses.
Using where for things that are not places.

content: Whose introduces possession in a relative clause and can refer to people, animals, or things.
examples: The student whose laptop was stolen called the police.
This is the company whose products are popular.
common_mistakes: Using who instead of whose for possession.
Adding his or her after whose.

content: When can introduce a relative clause that gives more information about a time.
examples: I remember the day when we first met.
Summer is the season when many people travel.
common_mistakes: Using where for time nouns.
Using when after nouns that are not time expressions.

content: Non-defining relative clauses add extra information and are separated by commas. They do not use that.
examples: My brother, who lives in Canada, is visiting us.
Paris, which is famous for art, attracts tourists.
common_mistakes: Using that in non-defining relative clauses.
Forgetting commas around extra information.

content: Whom is a formal object pronoun for people in relative clauses. In everyday English, who or that is often used instead.
examples: The man whom I saw is a teacher.
The woman who I met was friendly.
common_mistakes: Using whom as a subject pronoun.
Forgetting that object relative clauses have a subject after the pronoun.

content: Object relative pronouns can often be omitted in defining relative clauses. Subject relative pronouns cannot be omitted.
examples: The movie I watched was funny.
The book she bought is on the table.
common_mistakes: Omitting who when it is the subject.
Omitting where after place nouns when a preposition is needed.

content: Relative clauses follow normal clause word order after the relative pronoun. The pronoun is not followed by question word order.
examples: The girl who sits near me is kind.
The book that I bought is useful.
common_mistakes: Using question word order after who or which.
Putting the verb before the subject in object relative clauses.

content: A preposition can appear before the relative pronoun in formal style or at the end of the clause in informal style.
examples: The topic about which we spoke was complex.
The topic which we spoke about was complex.
common_mistakes: Using who after a fronted preposition in formal style.
Dropping the needed preposition completely.

content: Relative clauses can sometimes be reduced by removing the relative pronoun and changing the verb form.
examples: Students taking the test should be quiet.
The book written by her won a prize.
common_mistakes: Reducing clauses when the meaning becomes unclear.
Using an active participle for passive meaning.

content: Which can refer to a whole previous clause, especially in non-defining relative clauses.
examples: He arrived late, which annoyed everyone.
She passed the exam, which made her parents proud.
common_mistakes: Using what to refer to the whole previous clause.
Forgetting the comma before which.

content: In first conditional sentences, the if-clause uses present simple, not will, even though the meaning is future.
formula: if + present simple, will + base verb
examples: If he arrives early, he will call us.
If it rains, we will stay home.
common_mistakes: Using will in the if-clause.
Using past simple for a real future condition.

content: Unless means if not. It is used to introduce the only situation that will prevent something from happening.
examples: You will miss the bus unless you hurry.
Unless you study, you will fail.
common_mistakes: Adding another negative after unless.
Using unless when the meaning is simply because.

content: In formal second conditional sentences, were can be used with all subjects, especially in the phrase if I were you.
formula: if + subject + were, subject + would + base verb
examples: If I were you, I would apologize.
If she were here, she would know what to do.
common_mistakes: Using am in hypothetical conditions.
Using will instead of would for unreal present situations.

content: Mixed conditionals connect a condition in one time period with a result in another time period.
formula: if + past perfect, would + base verb
examples: If I had saved more money, I would buy a better car now.
If she had slept earlier, she would feel better now.
common_mistakes: Using would have for a present result.
Mixing time references without a clear meaning.

content: When the if-clause comes first, a comma usually separates it from the main clause. When the main clause comes first, a comma is usually not needed.
formula: if-clause, main clause / main clause if-clause
examples: If it rains, we will stay home.
We will stay home if it rains.
common_mistakes: Adding unnecessary commas before final if-clauses.
Forgetting the comma after an initial if-clause.

content: Provided that and as long as introduce conditions and mean if, but they often sound more specific or formal.
examples: You can join us as long as you arrive on time.
The plan will work provided that everyone helps.
common_mistakes: Using provided that for a reason instead of a condition.
Forgetting that the main clause still needs a complete verb.

content: Wish can express an unreal present situation. It commonly uses past simple after wish.
examples: I wish I had more free time.
She wishes she lived closer to school.
common_mistakes: Using present simple after wish for unreal present meaning.
Using will after wish for a present regret.

content: Wish can express regret about the past. It uses past perfect after wish.
examples: I wish I had studied harder.
They wish they had left earlier.
common_mistakes: Using past simple for past regrets.
Forgetting had before the past participle.

content: In case means because something might happen. It is not the same as if.
formula: main action + in case + possible situation
examples: Take an umbrella in case it rains.
I wrote down the address in case my phone died.
common_mistakes: Using in case when if is needed.
Treating in case as a direct condition for the result.

content: Should can be used in formal conditional clauses to suggest that something is possible but not very likely.
examples: Should you need help, contact reception.
Should the weather change, the event will move indoors.
common_mistakes: Using should inversion in casual beginner-level writing.
Combining should inversion with if.

content: If only expresses a strong wish or regret. It uses similar verb patterns to wish.
examples: If only I knew the answer.
If only we had arrived earlier.
common_mistakes: Using present simple after if only for unreal meaning.
Using if only for ordinary real conditions.

content: Pronouns often change in reported speech depending on who is speaking and who is being spoken about.
examples: Tom said, 'I like my job.' -> Tom said that he liked his job.
Anna said, 'My bag is new.' -> Anna said her bag was new.
common_mistakes: Keeping I when reporting another person's words.
Changing pronouns without checking the speaker.

content: Time expressions often change in reported speech when the reporting time is later than the original speech time.
formula: tomorrow -> the next day, yesterday -> the day before
examples: He said he would call the next day.
She said she had arrived the day before.
common_mistakes: Leaving tomorrow unchanged when the context has shifted.
Changing time expressions even when the context is still current.

content: Reported commands and requests commonly use told or asked plus object plus to-infinitive.
examples: The teacher told me to close the door.
She asked him to wait outside.
common_mistakes: Using that after told for commands.
Forgetting the object after told.

content: Negative reported commands use not before the to-infinitive.
formula: tell/ask + object + not + to + base verb
examples: He told me not to touch that.
The sign warned visitors not to enter.
common_mistakes: Using do not after told.
Putting not after to.

content: Say is usually used without a personal object, while tell is used with a personal object.
examples: She said that she was busy.
She told me that she was busy.
common_mistakes: Using said me.
Using told without an object.

content: Some modal verbs change in reported speech. Can often changes to could, and will often changes to would.
examples: Anna said she could swim.
He said he would help us.
common_mistakes: Keeping can after a past reporting verb when backshift is needed.
Using would after every modal.

content: Backshift is not always necessary when the reported information is still true or is a general truth.
formula: reporting verb + that + present tense for current truth
examples: The teacher said that water boils at 100 degrees Celsius.
She said she works in Hanoi, and she still does.
common_mistakes: Backshifting every reported statement mechanically.
Keeping present tense when the situation is no longer true.

content: Reported wh-questions keep the question word but use statement word order.
examples: She asked me where I lived.
He asked what I wanted.
common_mistakes: Keeping auxiliary question order.
Adding a question mark to an indirect question inside a statement.

content: Reported yes/no questions use if or whether and statement word order.
examples: He asked me if I spoke English.
She asked whether the train was late.
common_mistakes: Using do or did before the subject.
Using that instead of if or whether for yes/no questions.

content: Past continuous describes an action in progress at a specific time in the past or a longer action interrupted by a shorter one.
examples: I was cooking when the phone rang.
They were studying at 8 p.m.
common_mistakes: Using past continuous for a completed short action.
Using was with plural subjects.

content: Will is used for predictions, quick decisions, promises, and offers.
examples: I think it will rain later.
I will help you with your bag.
common_mistakes: Using will with to before the base verb.
Using will for every planned future action.

content: Be going to is used for plans and predictions based on present evidence.
formula: subject + am/is/are + going to + base verb
examples: We are going to visit our grandparents.
Look at the clouds. It is going to rain.
common_mistakes: Dropping the be verb before going to.
Using going to after will.

content: Present perfect can talk about life experiences without saying exactly when they happened.
examples: I have visited Japan.
Have you ever eaten sushi?
common_mistakes: Using past simple without a finished time expression.
Using the base verb after have or has.

content: Use since for a starting point and for for a duration with the present perfect.
examples: They have lived here since 2020.
She has worked there for five years.
common_mistakes: Using since with a duration.
Using for with a specific starting point.

content: Past perfect shows that one past action happened before another past action.
examples: By the time we arrived, the movie had started.
She had left before I called.
common_mistakes: Using present perfect for a sequence of past events.
Using past perfect when simple past is enough.

content: Stative verbs describe states, thoughts, feelings, possession, and senses. They are usually not used in continuous forms.
examples: I think this answer is correct.
She owns a small cafe.
common_mistakes: Using am thinking when think means believe.
Using continuous forms for possession verbs.

content: Present simple describes habits and facts, while present continuous describes actions happening now or temporary situations.
examples: She works in a bank.
She is working from home this week.
common_mistakes: Using present continuous for permanent routines.
Forgetting s in third-person present simple.

content: Past simple is used with finished time, while present perfect connects the past with the present.
formula: past simple + finished time / have-has + past participle
examples: I finished it yesterday.
I have finished it already.
common_mistakes: Using present perfect with yesterday.
Using past simple with ever for life experience questions.

content: Future continuous describes an action that will be in progress at a specific future time.
examples: This time tomorrow, I will be flying to Bangkok.
At 8 p.m., she will be studying.
common_mistakes: Using future continuous for a single completed future action.
Forgetting be after will.

content: Future perfect describes an action that will be completed before a specific time in the future.
examples: By next week, we will have finished the project.
She will have left by noon.
common_mistakes: Using will have with a base verb.
Confusing future perfect with present perfect.

content: Used to describes past habits or states that are no longer true.
examples: I used to play football after school.
She used to live near the beach.
common_mistakes: Using use to in affirmative sentences.
Using used to for current habits.

content: Be used to means be familiar with something. It is followed by a noun or gerund, not a base verb.
examples: I am used to waking up early.
They are used to the noise.
common_mistakes: Confusing be used to with used to.
Using a base verb after be used to.

content: Present perfect continuous emphasizes the duration or ongoing nature of an action that started in the past and continues or has present results.
examples: She has been studying for two hours.
It has been raining all morning.
common_mistakes: Using present continuous when duration from past to now is needed.
Forgetting been in the structure.

content: Prepositions of movement show direction. Use to for destination, into for entering, out of for leaving, and across for crossing.
examples: We are going to the airport.
She walked into the room.
They ran across the street.
common_mistakes: Using at for movement toward a destination.
Confusing in with into for movement.

content: During says when something happens within an event. For says how long something lasts.
examples: I slept during the flight.
I slept for two hours.
common_mistakes: Using during before a length of time.
Using for before an event noun when the meaning is within the event.

content: Since gives a starting point, while for gives a duration. They often appear with perfect tenses.
examples: She has lived here since 2021.
She has lived here for three years.
common_mistakes: Using since with durations.
Using for with exact starting times.

content: By means no later than a deadline. Until means continuing up to a time.
examples: Please submit the form by Friday.
We waited until midnight.
common_mistakes: Using until for a deadline action.
Using by for an action that continues.

content: Some adjectives take fixed prepositions. Good is usually followed by at before a skill or activity.
examples: He is good at solving problems.
She is good at tennis.
common_mistakes: Using good in for skills.
Using a base verb after at instead of a gerund.

content: Interested is followed by in. It can be followed by a noun or verb-ing form.
examples: She is interested in science.
They are interested in learning Spanish.
common_mistakes: Using interested on.
Using interested to before a base verb.

content: Depend is followed by on when something is affected or decided by another thing.
examples: The result depends on the weather.
Children depend on adults for support.
common_mistakes: Using depend of.
Dropping on after depend.

content: The noun reason is commonly followed by for when giving the cause or explanation of something.
examples: What is the reason for the delay?
There is no reason for worrying.
common_mistakes: Using reason of.
Using reason because as a noun phrase.

content: Between is often used for clearly separate people or things. Among is used when something is part of a group.
examples: The shop is between the bank and the cafe.
She found her keys among the papers.
common_mistakes: Using among for two clear items.
Using between when no separate items are identified.

content: Above and over both mean higher than, but over can also suggest covering, crossing, or movement from one side to another.
examples: The plane flew over the city.
The temperature is above zero.
common_mistakes: Using above for movement across something.
Using over when a measured scale needs above.

content: Transport vocabulary includes one-way ticket, round-trip ticket, platform, fare, route, schedule, and transfer.
examples: I need a round-trip ticket to Da Nang.
Which platform does the train leave from?
common_mistakes: Confusing one-way and round-trip.
Using price when fare is more specific for transport.

content: Travel document vocabulary includes passport, visa, identity card, boarding pass, travel insurance, and itinerary.
examples: You need a valid passport for international travel.
The visa allows visitors to stay for thirty days.
common_mistakes: Confusing visa with passport.
Using itinerary to mean passport.

content: Travel problem vocabulary includes delay, cancellation, lost luggage, missed connection, overbooking, and complaint.
examples: Our flight was delayed for two hours.
She reported her lost luggage at the service desk.
common_mistakes: Confusing delay with cancel.
Using luggage as a countable plural noun.

content: Direction phrases help travelers ask for and understand routes. Common phrases include turn left, turn right, go straight, cross the street, and next to.
examples: Go straight and turn left at the corner.
The museum is next to the station.
common_mistakes: Confusing left and right.
Using in front when next to is needed.

content: Booking phrases are used to reserve hotels, tickets, tours, or restaurant tables.
examples: I would like to book a room for two nights.
Do you have any available seats on Friday?
common_mistakes: Using reserve and preserve interchangeably.
Forgetting available when asking about open seats or rooms.

content: Airport security vocabulary includes security check, liquids, carry-on luggage, metal detector, and customs.
examples: Put your carry-on luggage on the belt.
You must go through customs after arrival.
common_mistakes: Confusing customs with customer.
Using luggage for only small personal bags when carry-on is more specific.

content: Hotel request phrases help guests ask for services politely, such as extra towels, a wake-up call, late check-out, or room service.
examples: Could I have a wake-up call at 6 a.m.?
Is late check-out available?
common_mistakes: Using command forms instead of polite requests.
Confusing check in and check out.

content: Tourist attraction vocabulary includes museum, landmark, monument, temple, beach, viewpoint, ticket office, and guided tour.
examples: The old temple is a famous landmark.
We joined a guided tour of the museum.
common_mistakes: Confusing monument and mountain.
Using travel when tourist attraction is intended.

content: Travel money vocabulary includes exchange rate, currency, cash, card, receipt, refund, and fee.
examples: What is the exchange rate today?
Keep the receipt in case you need a refund.
common_mistakes: Confusing currency with current.
Using refund when fee is intended.

content: Emergency travel vocabulary includes embassy, police station, hospital, lost passport, emergency number, and travel insurance claim.
examples: I lost my passport and need to contact the embassy.
Call the emergency number if you need urgent help.
common_mistakes: Confusing embassy with emergency.
Using insurance when claim is the action requested.

content: Anime-themed modal passive practice can use generic contexts such as episodes, manga chapters, character designs, studio schedules, reviews, spoilers, subtitles, and opening songs. Keep the grammar target as modal + be + past participle.
examples: The final episode should be watched after the recap.
Spoilers must be hidden before the review is posted.
The character design can be improved after feedback.
common_mistakes: Using modal + past participle without be.
Letting the anime context replace the grammar target.
Using specific franchise or character names when generic anime context is enough.

content: Past simple passive with plural subjects uses were plus the past participle. This form focuses on things that received an action in the past.
examples: The invitations were sent last week.
The windows were repaired yesterday.
common_mistakes: Using was with plural subjects.
Using were with the base verb instead of the past participle.

content: Present perfect is often used with just, already, and yet to talk about recent actions or expected actions connected to the present.
examples: She has just sent the email.
They have already finished the task.
Have you checked the file yet?
common_mistakes: Using the base verb after have or has.
Using past simple when the recent result is more important than the exact past time.

content: Future time clauses after when, before, after, as soon as, and until usually use present simple to refer to future time.
formula: main clause with will + when/before/after/as soon as/until + present simple
examples: I will call you when I get home.
We will start as soon as she arrives.
common_mistakes: Using will directly after when in a future time clause.
Using present continuous when a simple future time condition is intended.

content: Will is often used for predictions, offers, and quick decisions. Be going to is often used for plans and intentions.
formula: will + base verb / am-is-are going to + base verb
examples: I think it will rain later.
We are going to visit our grandparents this weekend.
common_mistakes: Using going to without the be verb.
Using will and going to together in the same verb phrase.

content: In defining relative clauses, the relative pronoun can sometimes be omitted when it is the object of the clause.
examples: The movie we watched last night was funny.
The book I borrowed is on the table.
common_mistakes: Omitting the relative pronoun when it is the subject.
Using where or who for an object that is a thing.

content: Relative clauses can include prepositions. In everyday English, the preposition often stays after the verb or adjective it belongs to.
formula: noun + relative pronoun + subject + verb + preposition
examples: The company that she works for is expanding.
This is the friend who I was talking about.
common_mistakes: Dropping the needed preposition.
Using where when a noun plus preposition structure is needed.

content: Mixed conditionals connect two different times. A common pattern links an unreal past condition with a present result.
formula: if + past perfect, would + base verb
examples: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
If she had taken the job, she would live in London now.
common_mistakes: Using would have for a present result.
Using past simple instead of past perfect for the unreal past condition.

content: Unless means if not. It is common in real conditions and is followed by an affirmative verb form.
formula: unless + present simple, will + base verb
examples: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.
We will go outside unless it rains.
common_mistakes: Using not after unless when the meaning is already negative.
Using will directly after unless in a first conditional clause.

content: Reported wh-questions keep the question word but use statement word order. The tense often backshifts after a past reporting verb.
formula: asked + object + question word + subject + verb
examples: He asked me where I lived.
She asked us what we wanted.
common_mistakes: Keeping auxiliary question order after the question word.
Using do or did in reported question word order.

content: Reported requests usually use asked plus an object plus a to-infinitive. Polite words such as please are not repeated in the same way.
examples: She asked me to wait there.
The teacher asked us to open our books.
common_mistakes: Using that after asked for a request.
Using a base verb instead of the to-infinitive.

content: Into shows movement from outside to inside a place. Out of shows movement from inside to outside.
examples: The cat jumped into the box.
She walked out of the room.
common_mistakes: Using in when movement into a place is intended.
Using from instead of out of for movement leaving an enclosed place.

content: Afraid is commonly followed by of before a noun or gerund when describing fear.
examples: Many children are afraid of the dark.
He is afraid of flying.
common_mistakes: Using afraid about for a general fear.
Using afraid to before a noun.

content: At the airport, a gate is the area where passengers wait before boarding. Boarding means getting onto a plane, train, or ship.
examples: Passengers should wait at Gate 12.
Boarding starts thirty minutes before departure.
common_mistakes: Confusing gate with check-in counter.
Using boarding pass to mean the physical place where passengers board.

content: Daily object vocabulary names common items used at home, school, and work, such as pen, notebook, key, bag, cup, plate, and phone.
examples: I use a pen to write on paper.
She put the keys in her bag.
common_mistakes: Confusing similar household objects.
Choosing a place or action when the question asks for an object.

content: Daily routine vocabulary describes common actions such as wake up, get dressed, have breakfast, go to school, study, work, and go to bed.
examples: I wake up at six o'clock.
They go to bed early on weekdays.
common_mistakes: Confusing wake up with get up.
Using sleep when wake up is required.

content: Work vocabulary includes deadline, meeting, task, schedule, manager, colleague, report, and project. These words are useful in office and study contexts.
examples: The deadline is Friday.
We have a meeting with our manager.
common_mistakes: Confusing deadline with timeline.
Using college when colleague is intended.

content: School vocabulary includes classmate, teacher, subject, homework, exam, lesson, classroom, and grade.
examples: A classmate is a person in the same class as you.
The teacher gave us homework.
common_mistakes: Confusing classmate with roommate.
Using student when the relationship in the same class is more specific.

content: Feeling vocabulary describes emotions and states such as happy, sad, nervous, excited, bored, tired, and worried.
examples: She felt nervous before the exam.
He was excited about the trip.
common_mistakes: Confusing nervous with hungry or tired.
Using boring when bored is needed for a person's feeling.

content: Technology vocabulary includes download, upload, file, device, password, screen, app, and internet connection.
examples: Download the file to your device.
Please enter your password.
common_mistakes: Confusing download and upload.
Using internet when a file or device is the specific word needed.
